title: Streams & Buffers
intro: Streams are how Node.js handles large or never-ending data with small, steady memory use, and Buffers are the raw bytes underneath. Interviewers ask about them because they separate people who have shipped file uploads, exports and proxies under load from people who have not. A senior answer talks about backpressure, error handling and cleanup with pipeline, and the memory cost of each choice.

questions.title: What streams are and why
questions.question: What is a stream in Node.js, and why would you use one instead of reading the whole file or body into memory?
questions.short: A stream is a way to handle data piece by piece (in chunks) as it arrives, instead of loading all of it into memory first. That keeps memory flat no matter how big the data is, and it lets you start sending or processing the first bytes right away, which improves time-to-first-byte. Streams also handle backpressure, so a fast producer cannot flood a slow consumer.
questions.simple: Reading a whole file is like filling a bathtub before you can use any water. A stream is like a tap: you use the water as it flows, and you never need a giant tub.

explain.p: With `fs.readFile`, Node reads the entire file into one Buffer and only then calls you. For a 2 GB file that means 2 GB of memory, and the client waits until the last byte is read before getting the first one.

With `fs.createReadStream`, Node reads the file in chunks (64 KB by default for file streams) and hands each chunk to you as soon as it is ready. You can write that chunk to the network straight away. Memory use stays around a few chunks, not the file size.

explain.caption: Same endpoint, two memory profiles

list: Memory: usage depends on chunk size and buffer limits, not on data size. 100 concurrent downloads of a 1 GB file do not need 100 GB.
Time-to-first-byte: the client starts receiving data after the first chunk is read, not after the whole file.
Composability: you can chain steps (read, gunzip, parse, transform, write) and each step only holds a little data at a time.

explain.p: Streams are everywhere in Node core: `http.IncomingMessage` (request body) is a Readable, `http.ServerResponse` is a Writable, TCP sockets are Duplex, and `zlib` and `crypto` objects are Transforms.

explain.note: Streams are not always the right tool. For a small JSON config file, `readFile` is simpler and just as fast. Reach for streams when data size is large, unknown, or unbounded (uploads, logs, exports, proxies).

anim.title: readFile vs createReadStream: memory over time

steps.note: readFile starts. Node reads the file, but nothing can be sent until all of it is loaded.
Memory keeps growing with every chunk read. The client is still waiting for its first byte.
Now the whole file sits in one big Buffer. For a 2 GB file, that is 2 GB of RAM per request.
Only now does res.end() send data. Time-to-first-byte equals the time to read the entire file.
Version B: the read stream fetches the first 64 KB chunk into its small internal buffer.
pipeline passes chunk 1 straight to the response. The client already has data.
The next chunk is read while the previous one is on the wire. Only a chunk or two live in memory.
This repeats. Memory stays flat because sent chunks can be garbage collected.
The last chunk is sent and the stream ends. Peak memory was a few chunks, not the file size.

followups.q: What is the default chunk size of fs.createReadStream?
followups.a: Its highWaterMark defaults to 64 KB (65536 bytes). Other byte streams default to 16 KB in Node 20 and 64 KB from Node 22; object-mode streams default to 16 objects.

followups.q: Is streaming always faster than readFile?
followups.a: Not for total throughput on small files; readFile can be slightly faster because it does fewer operations. Streams win on memory, time-to-first-byte, and when data is large or unbounded.

mistakes: Saying streams make code "faster" in general. The main win is bounded memory and earlier first byte, not raw CPU speed.
Using readFile or collecting the full request body for large uploads, which lets one big request exhaust memory.
Forgetting that HTTP requests and responses are already streams.

questions.title: The four stream types
questions.question: What are the four types of streams in Node.js? Give a real example of each.
questions.short: Readable is a source you read from, like fs.createReadStream or an HTTP request body. Writable is a destination you write to, like fs.createWriteStream or an HTTP response. Duplex is both readable and writable with two independent sides, like a TCP socket. Transform is a Duplex where the output is computed from the input, like zlib.createGzip or a CSV parser.
questions.simple: Readable is a tap, Writable is a drain, Duplex is a phone line (you talk and listen at the same time), and Transform is a water filter (what comes out depends on what went in).

head: Type
You...
Core examples
Implement
rows: write in, read out a changed version

explain.p: All of them are EventEmitters. Readables emit `data`, `end`, `error`, `close`. Writables emit `drain`, `finish`, `error`, `close`.

In a Duplex, the readable side and writable side are independent. On a TCP socket, what you write goes to the remote server and what you read comes from the remote server; they are not related inside your process. In a Transform, every byte you read out was produced from bytes you wrote in.

explain.caption: Compress a file with constant memory

explain.note: Client-side HTTP flips the roles: on `http.request`, the ClientRequest is Writable (you send the body) and the IncomingMessage response is Readable.

anim.title: Readable -> Transform -> Writable

steps.note: Readable.from turns an array into a Readable stream. Each element becomes one chunk.
The Transform is a Duplex: chunks go in on the writable side and changed chunks come out the readable side.
The Writable is the destination. Its write() is called once per chunk; cb() says "ready for the next one".
pipeline wires them together, but data only starts moving on a later tick, so the next line runs first.
Synchronous code runs to the end before any stream event fires.
"hello" flows into the Transform, which pushes "HELLO" out of its readable side.
The Writable receives "HELLO" and logs it.
The second chunk goes through the same path.
The Writable logs "STREAMS".
The source ends, end() propagates down, the Writable emits finish, and the pipeline promise resolves.

followups.q: Is process.stdout a Writable?
followups.a: Yes. Note that writes to stdout/stderr may be synchronous or asynchronous depending on whether it is a file, a TTY, or a pipe, and the platform.

followups.q: How do you create a custom stream without subclassing?
followups.a: Pass the implementation functions to the constructor, for example `new Transform({ transform(chunk, enc, cb) { ... } })`, or use `Readable.from()` with an iterable or async generator.

mistakes: Calling a socket a Transform. Its two sides are independent, so it is a Duplex.
Thinking a Transform must output one chunk per input chunk. It can push zero, one, or many.
Mixing up client and server roles for HTTP request/response streams.

questions.title: Flowing vs paused mode
questions.question: Explain flowing mode and paused mode for Readable streams. What switches a stream between them?
questions.short: A Readable starts in paused mode, where data sits in its buffer until you pull it with read() or attach a consumer. Attaching a data listener, calling resume(), or piping switches it to flowing mode, where Node pushes chunks to you as fast as they arrive. pause() or removing pipe destinations switches it back. In modern code you rarely manage this by hand: pipeline() and for await handle it for you.
questions.simple: Paused mode is a vending machine: nothing comes out until you press the button. Flowing mode is a conveyor belt: items keep coming until someone presses pause.

explain.p: Internally a Readable has `readableFlowing`, which can be `null`, `true`, or `false`. `null` means no consumer yet. `true` means flowing. `false` means explicitly paused.

head: Action
readableFlowing becomes
Effect
rows: starts flowing; with no data listener the data is lost
stops data events; data buffers up
you call read() in a loop

explain.caption: Paused mode: pull chunks yourself

explain.note: Calling `resume()` with no `data` listener and no pipe drains the stream and throws the data away. This is sometimes done on purpose, for example `res.resume()` on an HTTP client response you do not care about, so the socket is freed.

explain.p: Pausing a flowing stream does not stop the underlying source immediately. The stream keeps reading until its buffer reaches `highWaterMark`, then stops calling `_read()`. That is how pause gives you backpressure.
Async iteration (`for await (const chunk of readable)`) is the cleanest consumer: it pulls one chunk at a time, waits for your loop body, and destroys the stream if you `break` or throw.

anim.title: Switching modes

steps.note: A new Readable is created. It has data available but no consumer yet.
null means "nobody asked for data yet". Nothing is emitted.
Attaching a 'data' listener switches the stream to flowing mode. Chunks will be emitted on a later tick.
The flag flipped right away, but no data event has fired yet because we are still in synchronous code.
Data starts flowing. The first chunk "a" is delivered.
pause() switches to paused mode. "b" and "c" stay in the buffer instead of being emitted.
A timer is scheduled to resume later. Meanwhile the stream is quiet.
The timer fires and resume() switches back to flowing mode.
Buffered chunks are delivered in order.
No more data, so 'end' fires.

followups.q: What happens if you attach both 'readable' and 'data' listeners?
followups.a: 'readable' takes priority: the stream stays in paused mode and 'data' is only emitted when you call read(). Mixing styles is confusing, so pick one.

followups.q: Does pause() stop the file being read from disk?
followups.a: Not instantly. The stream fills its internal buffer up to highWaterMark and then stops calling _read(), so disk reads stop soon after.

mistakes: Calling resume() to "start" a stream without any data listener, which silently discards data.
Mixing on(data), on(readable), pipe and async iteration on the same stream.
Thinking a new stream starts emitting data on its own without a consumer.

questions.title: Backpressure and drain
questions.question: What is backpressure? Explain highWaterMark, what it means when write() returns false, and the drain event.
questions.short: Backpressure is the mechanism that stops a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer. Each Writable has a buffer with a highWaterMark limit; write() returns false once the buffered amount reaches that limit. A well-behaved producer then stops writing and waits for the drain event, which fires when the buffer has emptied. pipe() and pipeline() do this automatically; if you call write() in a loop and ignore the return value, memory grows without limit.
questions.simple: It is like filling cups at a coffee machine. When the tray is full, the machine says "stop" (write returns false). You wait until the tray is cleared (drain) before pouring more.

explain.p: `highWaterMark` is a threshold, not a hard cap. For byte streams it is a byte count; in object mode it is a count of objects (default 16). The default byte value was 16 KB up to Node 20 and became 64 KB in Node 22 (fs read streams have always used 64 KB), so check `writable.writableHighWaterMark` instead of hard-coding it.

`write()` always accepts the chunk and buffers it. The return value is advice: `true` means "below the threshold, keep going"; `false` means "at or above the threshold, please stop until drain". If you ignore it, the buffer just keeps growing in memory.

explain.caption: Manual writes that respect backpressure

explain.p: A Readable also has a buffer. When it is full, the stream stops calling `_read()` so the source is not read faster than it is consumed. pipe/pipeline connect the two: when the Writable says "full", the Readable is paused; on drain it resumes.

explain.note: Backpressure is the classic answer to "our proxy service used 6 GB of RAM": a fast upstream was copied into a slow client with manual `write()` calls that ignored the return value.

list: Use `writable.writableLength` to see how many bytes/objects are buffered.
Use `writable.writableNeedDrain` to check whether you should wait before writing.
Raise `highWaterMark` for throughput only when you understand the memory cost per stream times the number of concurrent streams.

anim.title: write() returns false, then drain

steps.note: A Writable with highWaterMark 3 bytes. Its write() is slow: each chunk takes 5ms to "flush".
write("0") goes straight to the slow write(). 1 byte is pending, below the limit, so it returns true.
write("1") is queued behind it. 2 bytes pending, still below 3, so true.
write("2") makes 3 bytes pending, which reaches highWaterMark. The chunk is still accepted, but write() returns false.
We respect the signal: stop the loop and wait for drain instead of piling up more data.
The slow destination finishes chunk 0 and calls cb(); chunk 1 starts.
Chunk 1 flushed. The buffer is shrinking, but drain waits until it is completely empty.
Chunk 2 flushed. The buffer is empty, so 'drain' fires and writeMore runs again.
We resume writing. "3" and "4" fit below the limit, so both return true.
end() is called. The remaining chunks flush, then 'finish' runs the callback.

followups.q: Does write() reject data when it returns false?
followups.a: No. The chunk is buffered either way. false is only a request to stop. Ignoring it makes the buffer grow without bound.

followups.q: What happens if you never wait for drain?
followups.a: Every chunk is buffered in memory. With a fast source and slow destination, the process memory grows until it crashes or is OOM-killed.

followups.q: How does pipe() implement backpressure?
followups.a: When dest.write() returns false, pipe calls src.pause(); when dest emits 'drain', it calls src.resume().

mistakes: Treating highWaterMark as a hard maximum; it is only the point where write() starts returning false.
Writing in a tight loop and ignoring the boolean returned by write().
Waiting for 'drain' when write() returned true; drain may never come and the code hangs.

questions.title: pipe vs pipeline
questions.question: What is the difference between readable.pipe() and stream.pipeline()? Which one should you use in production and why?
questions.short: pipe() handles backpressure but not errors: an error in one stream is not forwarded, and the other streams are not destroyed, which leaks file descriptors and sockets. pipeline() wires the same backpressure, but also forwards the first error to one callback or promise and destroys every stream in the chain. In production use pipeline from node:stream/promises with await and try/catch.
questions.simple: pipe() is a set of garden hoses taped together: if one bursts, the others keep running and you may not notice. pipeline() is a proper plumbing system with a shut-off valve: one leak shuts everything off and tells you.

explain.code:
// Fragile: errors are not forwarded, streams are not cleaned up
fs.createReadStream('in.csv')
  .pipe(zlib.createGzip())
  .pipe(fs.createWriteStream('out.gz'))
  .on('error', console.error); // only catches errors from the LAST stream

explain.caption: Production version

list: Pipes each stream into the next with backpressure.
Listens for error on every stream and reports the first one.
Destroys all streams when any one fails or the destination closes early, so file descriptors and sockets are released.
Resolves only after the last stream has finished, so "done" really means done.
Accepts async generator functions as steps, and an AbortSignal via options (`{ signal }`) for cancellation.

explain.caption: An async generator as a transform step

explain.note: In an HTTP handler, a client that disconnects mid-download makes `res` close early. pipeline then destroys the file stream for you. With pipe(), the file stream might stay open, which is a slow file-descriptor leak.

explain.p: `stream.finished(stream)` (or `require("node:stream/promises").finished`) is the companion helper: it tells you when a single stream is done or errored, which is useful when you cannot use pipeline.

anim.title: An error in the middle of a pipeline

steps.note: The source has three rows. The second one is bad.
pipeline connects source -> check -> sink and returns a promise. We await it inside try.
"row1" passes the check and is pushed on.
The sink writes "row1".
"BAD" reaches the Transform, which calls cb(err). The transform stream now errors.
pipeline sees the error and destroys every stream in the chain, so nothing leaks. row3 is never written.
The pipeline promise rejects with the first error, so a normal try/catch handles it.
Both ends really were destroyed. With pipe() the source would still be open and the error would be unhandled.

followups.q: How do you cancel a pipeline?
followups.a: Pass an AbortSignal: `await pipeline(a, b, c, { signal })`. Aborting destroys all streams and rejects with an AbortError.

followups.q: What if I need the destination to stay open, e.g. writing several files into one socket?
followups.a: pipeline accepts an `end: false` option for the destination in newer versions; otherwise write manually with backpressure handling and stream.finished for errors.

mistakes: Adding .on('error') only at the end of a .pipe() chain and assuming it catches errors from every stream.
Using callback pipeline and forgetting to handle the error argument.
Assuming pipe() closes the source when the destination fails.

questions.title: Writing a Transform stream
questions.question: Write a Transform stream that splits incoming text into lines. What edge cases matter?
questions.short: Extend Transform and implement _transform(chunk, encoding, callback). Chunk boundaries are arbitrary, so keep the last partial line in a buffer, prepend it to the next chunk, push each complete line, and call callback once per chunk. Implement _flush to push the leftover partial line when the input ends. Use readableObjectMode so each pushed line is one chunk.
questions.simple: Chunks are like pages torn at random spots. You keep the half-sentence at the bottom of each page and glue it to the top of the next page before reading it.

explain.p: The key insight is that a chunk is not a line, a record, or a JSON object. It is just whatever bytes were available, so it can cut a line (or even a multi-byte UTF-8 character) in half.

explain.caption: Line splitter Transform

list: Call the callback exactly once per chunk. Calling it twice errors the stream with ERR_MULTIPLE_CALLBACK; never calling it stalls the stream.
Pass an error as `callback(err)` instead of throwing. That errors the stream so pipeline can clean up.
`this.push(x)` may be called zero or many times. `callback(null, x)` is a shortcut for push(x) then callback().
`_flush(callback)` runs after the last chunk, before end. Use it to emit buffered leftovers.
Multi-byte characters split across chunks: use `string_decoder` or `setEncoding("utf8")` upstream instead of `chunk.toString()` on raw bytes. (The example uses ASCII for clarity.)
Windows line endings: split on `/\r?\n/`.
A huge line with no newline: the tail grows without limit. Add a maximum line length and error out if exceeded.
Empty trailing line after the final newline: only push the tail if it is non-empty.

explain.note: For most real line-reading jobs, `readline` with `for await` is simpler. Write your own Transform when you need it inside a pipeline with custom logic.

anim.title: Chunks are not lines

steps.note: The splitter starts with an empty tail. Its readable side is in object mode, so each line is one chunk.
Attaching 'data' puts the readable side in flowing mode.
First chunk arrives: "ab\ncd". It contains one full line and the start of another.
Split on newline gives ["ab", "cd"]. The last piece may be incomplete, so pop it into the tail.
Only the complete line "ab" is pushed and delivered.
Second chunk: "e\nf". The tail "cd" is glued to the front first.
"cd" + "e\nf" = "cde\nf", which splits into ["cde", "f"]. "f" becomes the new tail.
"cde" is complete. A naive splitter would have wrongly emitted "cd" and "e".
end() means no more input. Before finishing, Node calls _flush.
_flush pushes the leftover tail "f" so the last line is not lost.

followups.q: How would you make this safe for UTF-8?
followups.a: Create a `StringDecoder('utf8')` from node:string_decoder, call decoder.write(chunk) in _transform and decoder.end() in _flush. It holds back incomplete multi-byte sequences.

followups.q: How do you signal an error from a Transform?
followups.a: Call callback(err). The stream emits error, and pipeline destroys all streams and rejects.

mistakes: Assuming each chunk is exactly one line or one JSON object.
Forgetting _flush, which silently drops the last line when the file does not end with a newline.
Throwing inside _transform instead of passing the error to the callback.

questions.title: Object mode
questions.question: What is object mode in streams, and how does it change highWaterMark and backpressure?
questions.short: By default streams carry only Buffers or strings (or Uint8Array). With objectMode: true, a stream can carry any JavaScript value except null, one value per chunk. highWaterMark then counts objects instead of bytes, defaulting to 16. Backpressure still works, but it is counted per object, so 16 huge objects can still use a lot of memory.
questions.simple: A normal stream is a pipe carrying water measured in litres. An object-mode stream is a conveyor belt carrying boxes, and the limit is "16 boxes", no matter how heavy each box is.

explain.caption: Filtering objects in a pipeline

explain.p: You can set object mode on one side of a Transform only: `readableObjectMode: true` (bytes in, objects out, like a CSV parser) or `writableObjectMode: true` (objects in, bytes out, like a serializer).
`null` cannot be pushed as data, because `push(null)` means "end of stream". If you need a "nothing" value, wrap it.

explain.note: If each object is a 5 MB record, 16 of them buffered at each stage of a 4-stage pipeline can mean hundreds of MB. Lower highWaterMark for large objects.

explain.p: Database drivers and parsers often expose object-mode Readables (for example a query cursor stream), which let you process millions of rows with bounded memory.

anim.title: Objects through a filter

steps.note: Readable.from with an array of objects creates an object-mode Readable automatically.
The Transform is in object mode on both sides, so it receives the objects as-is, not as bytes.
In object mode, highWaterMark counts objects. The default is 16.
pipe() connects them and the data listener starts the flow on a later tick.
Ann is 34, so her name is pushed. One object in, a string out.
Bob is 15. Nothing is pushed; cb() alone just says "done with this one". A Transform can drop items.
Cy is 41 and passes the filter.
The source ends, the Transform ends, and 'end' fires.

followups.q: Can you pipe an object-mode stream into fs.createWriteStream?
followups.a: Not directly. The file stream expects strings or Buffers, so it throws on plain objects. Put a serializer Transform (for example JSON.stringify(obj) + newline) in between.

followups.q: Can you push undefined or 0 in object mode?
followups.a: Yes, any value except null is allowed. null always means end of stream.

mistakes: Assuming highWaterMark 16 in object mode limits memory; it limits count, not size.
Pushing null as a data value and accidentally ending the stream.
Forgetting objectMode and getting ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE ("The \"chunk\" argument must be of type string or an instance of Buffer...") errors.

questions.title: Huge file line by line
questions.question: How would you process a 20 GB log file line by line in Node.js without running out of memory?
questions.short: Create a read stream with fs.createReadStream, wrap it with readline.createInterface using crlfDelay: Infinity, and consume it with for await...of. Only a small buffer is in memory at any time, and because for await waits for your loop body, any async work you do per line naturally applies backpressure. Never use readFile or split the whole content.
questions.simple: You read the book one line at a time with your finger on the page, instead of photocopying the whole book first.

explain.caption: Count error lines with constant memory

explain.p: `crlfDelay: Infinity` makes readline treat `\r\n` as one line break even if `\r` and `\n` arrive in different chunks.

explain.h: Why for await is the right consumer

list: It reads one line, runs your body (including any awaits), then pulls the next. A slow DB insert per line slows reading down instead of buffering lines.
If you break or throw, the loop closes the readline interface. It does not destroy the input file stream, so call `input.destroy()` (for example in a `finally`) if you stop early.
Errors from the underlying stream are thrown inside the loop, so try/catch works.

explain.note: readline has its own small internal line buffer and may read ahead a bit. For strict throughput, batch inserts (e.g. 1,000 lines per DB call) instead of one await per line; that is often 10-100x faster.

explain.p: If the file is gzipped, put `zlib.createGunzip()` between the file stream and readline: `readline.createInterface({ input: fs.createReadStream(f).pipe(zlib.createGunzip()) })` (or use pipeline into a PassThrough to get proper error handling).

anim.title: readline + for await

steps.note: For the demo we write a small log file. Imagine it is 20 GB.
createReadStream opens the file. It will read chunks (64 KB each) only when someone pulls.
readline wraps the byte stream and splits it into lines, handling lines that cross chunk borders.
for await pulls the first line. The loop body runs before the next line is pulled.
Line 2 starts with ERROR, so we count it and log it.
Line 3 is INFO. Only one line is held by our code at a time; earlier lines can be garbage collected.
Line 4 is another ERROR.
The stream hits end of file, so the async iterator finishes and the loop exits.
We print the summary. Peak memory was one chunk plus one line, regardless of file size.

followups.q: How would you speed it up with multiple CPU cores?
followups.a: Split the file into byte ranges (createReadStream with start/end), align each range to the next newline, and process ranges in worker threads or child processes, then merge results.

followups.q: How do you handle a malformed line without stopping?
followups.a: Wrap the per-line parse in try/catch, count or log the bad line, and continue. Only let truly fatal errors escape the loop.

mistakes: Using fs.readFileSync(file).toString().split('\n') on a large file.
Using rl.on('line', async ...) and assuming awaits inside the handler pause reading. They do not; the lines keep coming.
Inserting one row per await for millions of lines instead of batching.

questions.title: Streaming HTTP downloads and uploads
questions.question: How do you stream a large file download to an HTTP client, and how do you accept a large upload without buffering it in memory?
questions.short: For downloads, set headers (Content-Type, Content-Length if known, Content-Disposition), then pipeline a file read stream into the response; pipeline handles backpressure from slow clients and destroys the file stream if the client disconnects. For uploads, treat req as a Readable and pipeline it to disk or object storage, with a size limit enforced while streaming. Never collect the body into one Buffer for large payloads.
questions.simple: Instead of loading the whole truck into your garage and then driving it to the customer, you put a conveyor belt from your shelves to their door.

explain.caption: Streaming download
Streaming upload with a size limit

list: Reject early using the Content-Length header when present, but still count bytes while streaming because the header can lie or be absent (chunked encoding).
For multipart/form-data uploads, use a streaming parser such as busboy instead of one that writes everything to memory.
Compressing on the fly (`zlib.createGzip()` in the pipeline) means you cannot know Content-Length in advance; Node then uses chunked transfer encoding.
If you proxy to object storage (e.g. S3), use the SDK's streaming/multipart upload so the body is never fully buffered.

explain.note: A slow mobile client is the real backpressure test: the response socket buffer fills, `res.write()` returns false, and pipeline pauses the file read. Without it, the whole file would be read into memory waiting for the slow client.

anim.title: Download to a slow client

steps.note: stat gives the file size, so we can send Content-Length and the browser can show progress.
Headers go out first. The client already knows a download has started.
The read stream fetches the first chunk from disk.
pipeline writes c1 to res. The socket sends it to the client.
The client is on slow mobile data. Chunks pile up in the response buffer until it hits highWaterMark.
Because res.write() returned false, pipeline pauses the file stream. Disk reading stops; memory stays bounded.
The client catches up. 'drain' fires and pipeline resumes reading the file.
Now the user closes the tab. The response emits close before finishing.
pipeline destroys the file stream, which closes its file descriptor, and the await rejects with ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE.

followups.q: How would you support resumable downloads?
followups.a: Handle the Range header: parse start/end, reply 206 with Content-Range, and use fs.createReadStream(file, { start, end }) (end is inclusive).

followups.q: Why not use express.json() or body-parser for uploads?
followups.a: They buffer the whole body into memory to parse it. They are fine for small JSON with a size limit, but large files should be streamed.

mistakes: Collecting upload chunks into an array and Buffer.concat-ing them.
Trusting Content-Length alone as the upload size limit.
Using pipe() for downloads and leaking file descriptors when clients abort.
Leaving partially written files on disk after a failed upload.

questions.title: Buffer basics
questions.question: What is a Buffer? Explain encodings, Buffer.from vs Buffer.alloc vs Buffer.allocUnsafe, and why string length can differ from buffer length.
questions.short: A Buffer is a fixed-size chunk of raw bytes, a subclass of Uint8Array, usually stored outside the V8 heap. Buffer.from copies data from a string, array or buffer; Buffer.alloc creates a zero-filled buffer; Buffer.allocUnsafe is faster but may contain old memory, so you must overwrite it fully. A string's length counts UTF-16 code units, while a buffer's length counts bytes, so "héllo" is 5 characters but 6 bytes in UTF-8. Slicing a buffer with subarray shares memory with the original.
questions.simple: A string is the text you read; a Buffer is the raw bytes on disk or on the wire. Some letters, like é or emoji, take more than one byte, so the byte count can be bigger than the letter count.

head: API
What you get
When to use
rows: new bytes, encoded from the string
when you need an independent copy
hot paths where you overwrite every byte

explain.note: `allocUnsafe` can return memory that used to hold other data, such as passwords or tokens from another request. If you send such a buffer without filling it completely, you leak data. That is exactly why `new Buffer(n)` was deprecated.

explain.p: Common encodings: `utf8` (default), `hex`, `base64`, `base64url`, `latin1`, `ascii`, `utf16le`. Encoding only matters when converting between strings and bytes: `Buffer.from(str, enc)` and `buf.toString(enc)`.

`buf.subarray()` and the deprecated `buf.slice()` both return a view over the same bytes. Changing the view changes the original. This differs from `Array.prototype.slice`, which copies. Small buffers may also share one big pre-allocated pool, so `buf.buffer` (the underlying ArrayBuffer) may be larger than your buffer; always use `buf.byteOffset` and `buf.length` with it.

Memory accounting: Buffer contents usually live outside the JS heap and show up in `process.memoryUsage().external` and `arrayBuffers`, not `heapUsed`. That is why a process can have a small heap but large RSS.

explain.note: Keeping a tiny `subarray` of a huge buffer keeps the whole huge buffer alive. If you keep a small slice long term, copy it with `Buffer.from(slice)` so the big one can be freed.

anim.title: Bytes, encodings and shared memory

steps.note: A JS string with 5 characters. é is one UTF-16 code unit, so length is 5.
Encoding as UTF-8: é needs two bytes (c3 a9), so the buffer has 6 bytes.
Character count and byte count differ. Use Buffer.byteLength for headers like Content-Length.
console.log shows the raw bytes in hex.
The same bytes can be shown as hex or base64 text. The bytes do not change, only the text view.
subarray(0, 1) does NOT copy. part is a window onto the first byte of buf.
Writing 0x4a ('J') through part changes buf too, because they share memory.
Buffer.from(buf) makes a real copy. Changing copy[0] to 'M' leaves buf alone.
Two independent buffers now.
Buffer.alloc always zero-fills. allocUnsafe would skip this and might show old data.

followups.q: Why is Buffer.allocUnsafe faster?
followups.a: It skips zero-filling, and for small sizes (under half of Buffer.poolSize, 8 KB by default) it slices from a pre-allocated pool, avoiding a new allocation.

followups.q: How do you safely join many chunks?
followups.a: Collect them in an array and call Buffer.concat(chunks, totalLength) once. Do not use string concatenation on binary data; it corrupts multi-byte characters split across chunks.

followups.q: How do you compare secrets held in buffers?
followups.a: Use crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b) with equal-length buffers to avoid timing attacks, not buf.equals or ===.

mistakes: Using str.length for Content-Length; it must be Buffer.byteLength(str).
Assuming buf.slice() copies like Array.slice.
Using allocUnsafe and not overwriting all bytes, leaking old memory contents.
Concatenating chunk.toString() per chunk, which breaks characters split between chunks.

questions.title: Readable.from and async generators
questions.question: How do Readable.from() and async generators relate to streams? When would you use them?
questions.short: Readable.from() turns any iterable or async iterable, including an async generator, into a Readable stream (object mode by default). Readables are themselves async iterables, so you can consume them with for await. Together they let you write producers and transforms as plain async functions with yield, and pipeline accepts async generator functions as steps, so you get backpressure and cleanup without subclassing stream classes.
questions.simple: An async generator is a function that hands out items one at a time when asked. Readable.from puts a stream "wrapper" around it so it plugs into any pipe.

explain.caption: Paginated API exposed as a stream

explain.p: The generator only runs when the stream asks for more data, so a slow consumer slows the producer. However, the stream keeps a small read-ahead buffer (up to highWaterMark), so the producer may run a few items ahead of the consumer. You can see this in the animation: page 2 is fetched before page 1 is handled.

list: Turning a paginated API or DB cursor into a stream of records.
Generating test data or CSV exports: `Readable.from(rowsGenerator())`.
Writing transform steps as `async function* (source) { for await (const x of source) yield f(x); }` inside pipeline.
Converting a string or Buffer into a stream (note: a string is emitted as ONE chunk, not character by character).

explain.caption: Export with no custom stream classes

explain.note: If the consumer breaks out of a `for await` early, the stream is destroyed and the generator's `finally` block runs. Put cleanup (closing a cursor, releasing a connection) in `finally`.

explain.p: Readables also have iterator-style helpers such as `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.take()`, `.toArray()` (still marked experimental in the docs). They are handy for small tasks, but `toArray()` collects everything into memory.

anim.title: Async generator behind a stream

steps.note: Readable.from wraps the async generator. Nothing runs yet; generators are lazy.
for await asks the stream for data. The stream asks the generator for its first item.
The generator "fetches" page 1 and yields it into the stream buffer.
The stream reads ahead to fill its buffer, so the generator is resumed and fetches page 2 before page 1 is handled.
The loop body handles page 1.
Buffer has room again, so the stream pulls page 3 from the generator.
Page 2 is handled.
Page 3 is handled. The generator loop ended, so the stream ends after this item.
for await finishes when the stream ends.

followups.q: Why might you iterate the generator directly instead of wrapping it?
followups.a: If you only need to loop over items in one place, a plain for await over the generator is simpler and has no read-ahead. Wrap it with Readable.from when you need to plug it into stream APIs like pipe, pipeline, or an HTTP response.

followups.q: What does Readable.from("hello") emit?
followups.a: One chunk, "hello". Strings and Buffers are not iterated character by character by Readable.from.

mistakes: Expecting the producer to run strictly one item at a time; streams read ahead up to highWaterMark.
Putting cleanup after the loop in a generator instead of in finally, so it is skipped on early exit.
Using .toArray() on a huge stream and losing all the memory benefits.

questions.title: Common stream bugs
questions.question: What are the most common bugs you have seen with Node.js streams, and how do you avoid them?
questions.short: The big ones are: missing error handlers, which crash the process with an unhandled error event; using pipe() without cleanup, which leaks file descriptors when a client aborts; ignoring write() returning false, which causes unbounded memory; async work in data or line handlers that does not pause the stream; forgetting to call the callback in _transform or calling it twice; and treating chunks as lines or JSON objects. Using pipeline, for await, and stream helpers avoids almost all of them.
questions.simple: Most stream bugs come from three forgotten things: catching errors, cleaning up when something stops early, and waiting when the other side says "slow down".

head: Bug
Symptom
Fix
rows: use pipeline or attach error handlers
file descriptors / sockets leak, EMFILE later
call cb exactly once, on every path
split with a buffer tail or use readline
Responding on 'end' of a write stream

explain.h: Events: end vs finish vs close

list: 'end' is on Readables: all data has been consumed.
'finish' is on Writables: end() was called and all data has been flushed to the underlying system.
'close' fires after the underlying resource (fd, socket) is closed. Both sides may emit it. With autoDestroy (default true), streams are destroyed after end/finish.

explain.note: Errors also bubble differently: an error on a stream does NOT propagate along a pipe() chain. Every stream in a pipe chain needs its own handler, which is the main reason pipeline exists.

explain.p: Debug tip: when a stream "hangs", check `readable.readableFlowing`, `readable.readableLength`, `writable.writableLength`, and `writable.writableNeedDrain`. A hang usually means a missing callback, a paused stream nobody resumes, or a drain that never comes because nothing is consuming the destination.

anim.title: Async 'data' handler vs for await

steps.note: Version A: a 'data' handler is attached and the stream starts flowing.
r1 arrives and starts an insert. The handler returns a promise right away, and the stream does not wait for it.
The stream immediately emits r2, r3, r4... Each starts another insert in parallel.
With a million rows, that is a million concurrent queries: pool exhaustion, memory spikes, and unhandled rejections.
Version B: for await pulls only r1. The rest stays buffered or unread on disk.
The loop awaits the insert. The stream fills its buffer to highWaterMark and then stops reading.
r1 is done. Only now is r2 pulled. Exactly one insert is in flight.
This continues at the speed of the database. Memory and concurrency stay bounded, and an error throws out of the loop.

followups.q: How would you process rows with limited concurrency, say 10 at a time?
followups.a: Use readable.map(fn, { concurrency: 10 }) (experimental helper), or a small manual pool inside for await that waits when 10 promises are in flight.

followups.q: Why might 'finish' fire but the file still be open?
followups.a: 'finish' means data was handed to the OS. The file descriptor is closed later; wait for 'close' if you need to rename or delete the file right after.

mistakes: Assuming an error on one stream travels along a pipe() chain.
Treating 'end' and 'finish' as the same event.
Running async work inside on('data') or on('line') and thinking the stream waits.
